The Oba of Ado and Olofin Adimula Oodua of Aworiland, Oba Olusola Lamidi-Osolo, has proposed a structured cultural partnership between Nigeria and Brazil, seeking joint academic research, diaspora exchanges and legal protection for Yoruba heritage sites and traditions. The monarch said historical ties between the two countries should move beyond symbolic recognition to practical measures that would preserve Yoruba cultural identity among Afro-Brazilian communities and pass indigenous knowledge to future generations. He made the proposal while delivering a royal address, titled “The Role of Traditional Leadership in Modern Cultural Sustainability and the Safeguarding of Sacred Heritage,” at the Universidade Federal Fluminense in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, recently. Addressing academics, researchers, students, traditional rulers and Afro-Brazilian community leaders, Lamido-Osolo identified the Nago/Anago identity, Candomble practices, the veneration of Orisa such as Sango, Osun, Yemoja and Ogun, and culinary traditions including Acarajé, known in Yoruba as Akara, as evidence of the enduring influence of African culture in Brazil. “Africa and Brazil may be separated by the Atlantic Ocean, but the ocean could not extinguish the memory of our ancestors,” he said. These include structured exchanges involving traditional rulers, scholars, artists and community leaders; joint university research into Yoruba linguistics, genealogy, oral history and gastronomy; and diaspora immersion programmes through which Afro-descendants in Brazil could visit Ado-Odo in Ogun State to explore their ancestral connections. He also advocated digital archives and legal frameworks to protect sacred sites and living traditions from neglect and commercial exploitation, alongside youth mentorship, student exchanges and cultural entrepreneurship initiatives. The proposals place traditional institutions at the centre of efforts to connect historical memory with contemporary cultural preservation. A crown is not simply an ornament of royalty; it represents an enduring covenant between the ancestors, the living and generations yet unborn,” he said. He cited the traditional governance structure of Ado-Odo, which he said originated around 1050 AD from Ile-Ife, as an example of institutional participation in traditional leadership. The monarch identified the Oba-in-Council, Afobaje (Kingmakers) and Itepa Ilu (Town Council) as components of the kingdom’s governance structure, which he said maintained institutional balance across its four quarters. The monarch also linked cultural preservation to environmental protection, warning that the destruction of natural surroundings could undermine the traditions and spiritual practices associated with sacred sites. “When we destroy the natural environment of a sacred tradition, we risk destroying part of the tradition itself,” he said. He identified 16 indigenous shrines, 16 Igbi-Ora drums and sacred natural sites, including Odo Iji, in Ado-Odo as heritage assets requiring coordinated conservation. On the ethical responsibilities of traditional leadership, he invoked the Yoruba philosophy of Omoluabi, stressing that integrity, truthfulness, character and human dignity should guide community leadership. The monarch concluded by inviting academics, students and members of the Afro-Brazilian community to attend the forthcoming Oduduwa Awori Festival in Ado-Odo, Ogun State, as part of efforts to deepen cultural engagement between the two countries.
